evidence.snippet: - `dispose` first writes a disposal mark to the cell, and `add` refuses a changeset whose cell holds one. Disposal is permanent: the port has no way to recreate a changeset, since one would need an incarnation every record and writer carries.

Closing a pull request still disposes nothing, and `dispose` keeps its meaning: a writer's own command removes a changeset for good and marks it.

### Retirement

`GitRecordStore.retire(seen)` takes changeset names, each with the tree ID its folder had when the caller decided. In one commit it removes each folder whole, cell included, with no mark. A retired changeset is the same as one never written, so a reopened pull request records again from nothing. Retiring a disposed changeset takes its mark too, so a retirement undoes a disposal. That is wanted: a retirement leaves the tip as if the pull request never recorded, and a disposal's purpose, removing a changeset's records from the tip for good, holds once the job has retired it.

verification.reason: Base rule 3 of the shared-record decision (line 107) says that after `dispose`, `add` refuses the changeset, that disposal is permanent, and that the port cannot recreate a changeset without an incarnation on every record and writer. At head, `retire` calls `judgeFolder`, which treats a disposed folder as clean when it holds nothing stray. `withoutFolders` then removes the whole folder, mark included. `removesOnly` accepts that commit, and nothing in the retire path checks for a disposal mark. The head's own test (retire.test.ts:593) shows `add` failing with `disposed` before the retire and succeeding after it. The new decision (lines 3-5) amends rule 13 and the git-record-store decision. It does not amend rule 3's permanence clause, yet line 33 undoes it and line 29 says `dispose` "keeps its meaning". A head decision cannot excuse a departure from base. The base reason, that no incarnation tells a recreated changeset's records apart from a late writer's, is untouched by the head. Retirement still lets a late writer land into a changeset that had been refused. The late-writer step is inferred, but the weakening of the fail-closed refusal is traced in code.
